h1: Beer knowledge for drinks marketing teams
title: Beer knowledge for marketing teams | Craft Beer School
desc: What marketers should know about beer to write accurate claims: styles, ingredients, bitterness, ABV, freshness, craft and non-alcoholic labelling.
teaser: A campaign that gets the product wrong loses brewers and informed drinkers at once. A little product knowledge goes a long way.
standfirst: Marketing teams write about beer without making it. This guide covers the facts that are easiest to get wrong and why they matter.
sections:
Brewers, bartenders and informed drinkers notice mistakes. Calling an ale a lager, or describing bitterness as strength, makes a brand look like it does not know its own product. Regulators also care about claims. Rules on alcohol advertising and labelling differ by country and change, so your compliance team has the last word.

The cost of an error is rarely a fine. It is a lost conversation with the brewers and bar staff who recommend your beer to others.

Ask the brewery for a one-page fact sheet for each product: style, ABV, ingredients, serving temperature and the flavour words the brewer uses. Keep it beside every brief.

A beer style is a family with shared ingredients and methods. Lagers are fermented cold and taste clean. Ales are fermented warmer and show more yeast character. Wheat beers use a good share of wheat. Stouts and porters use roasted malt. Sours have lactic acidity. Style names are shorthand for expectations, so use them carefully. Our beer styles guide is a good reference.

Packaging and serving language matters too. Draught, keg, cask, can and bottle carry different expectations. A cask ale is served at cellar temperature with low carbonation, while a keg lager is served cold and fizzy. Do not mix them up in copy.

Seasonal and limited releases need the same care. A winter beer is usually stronger or maltier, not just given a festive label. Use the name of the style that is really in the tank.
Bitterness, strength and body are different

IBU measures bitterness compounds from hops. ABV measures alcohol. Neither tells you the other. A dark stout can be low in alcohol. A pale beer can be strong. Perceived bitterness also depends on sweetness and body: a malty beer with 40 IBU may taste less bitter than a thin one at 30. Do not use bitterness as a proxy for quality or strength.

A quick check helps: before publishing a description, read it aloud and ask a brewer whether it matches what is in the glass.

Water, malt, hops and yeast are the base. Claims such as natural, handcrafted or small batch carry meaning to drinkers. Some are regulated. Check them with the brewery. Do not invent origin stories. Avoid health claims entirely: they are inaccurate for beer and legally risky in many places.

Ingredient lists and allergen information are regulated in many countries. Barley and wheat contain gluten. Some beers use added flavourings. Leave this to compliance review.

Beer is perishable. Hop aroma fades, oxygen causes stale flavours and heat accelerates both. Marketing materials that show beer left in the sun or on warm shelves send the wrong message to informed buyers. If you feature a date, make sure the brewery agrees it.

Photography deserves a line. Sprayed-on condensation and an impossibly perfect foam head are common in drinks photography. Make sure the claims alongside the picture are true.
Craft is a story, not a standard

Craft means different things in different countries. Some definitions refer to size or independence, others to flavour or method. Know which one your brand claims and be ready to defend it. See what is craft beer.

Words like premium or craft do not describe taste. Pair them with something concrete such as the malt, the hop or the fermentation, so that the claim can be tested in the glass.

Labels for non-alcoholic beer are regulated and differ across countries. Use only the descriptor your regulator allows. Check taste claims with brewers: dealcoholised and limited-fermentation beers differ, as explained in non-alcoholic beer styles explained.

Use consistent terms in briefs. When the brief says crisp, you should be able to say which beer is crisp and why.

Remember also that not everyone drinks. A balanced campaign includes options and respectful imagery for drinkers and non-drinkers alike.

Marketers who have tasted, toured and asked questions write better. A short programme combining product basics and a guided tasting, run live online or on site, gives a team the vocabulary to brief agencies and review copy. See sensory training for sales teams and brewery KPIs for related sessions.
faqs: What should marketers know first about beer?
Styles, the difference between bitterness and strength, freshness and the limits on claims.
Is IBU a measure of strength?
No. IBU measures bitterness compounds. ABV measures alcohol. They are unrelated.
Can I make health claims about beer?
No. They are inaccurate and often illegal. Keep to flavour, craft and occasion.
It can, as an optional and responsible part, with non-alcoholic choices and spit cups.
